title: Asch's Lines
objective: After this level you can explain Solomon Asch's conformity experiments and what made people more or less likely to go along.
summary: In Asch's 1950s line studies, about three in four people went along with an obviously wrong group answer at least once. One ally or a private answer weakened the pull.

cards.headline: Which line matches? Easy, until everyone else answers first.
cards.body: In the 1950s, Solomon Asch gave groups a vision test a child could pass. The catch was the other people at the table. What made careful adults say something they could see was false, and what set them free?

cards.headline: The rigged vision test
cards.body: Asch showed a target line and three others, and each person said aloud which one matched. Only one person at the table was a real participant. The rest were confederates, people working for the researcher, and on some trials they all named an obviously wrong line. Then the real participant had to answer. In Asch's 1955 report, 76 percent went along with the wrong answer at least once. Three in four, on a test a child could pass.

cards.headline: Saying it without believing it
cards.body: Conformity means changing your behavior to go along with a group, even when you disagree. Asch's participants weren't confused. The task was easy, so they didn't need the group for information. They said the wrong answer out loud while privately not accepting it, to fit in and avoid ridicule. Psychologists call that normative social influence: going along to get along.

mascot.line: People mix up agreeing and going along. Asch's participants mostly went along: the words changed, the belief didn't.

cards.headline: What turns the pressure up or down

items.label: A bigger majority
points: Only up to a point, then it stopped rising

items.label: One ally
points: A single dissenter from the majority

cards.headline: Asch's lines
learned: Confederates gave obviously wrong answers aloud
About three in four went along at least once
They went along to fit in, not from doubt
One ally or a private answer weakened the pull

questions.prompt: In Asch's 1955 report, what share of participants went along with the group's wrong answer at least once?

options.label: About 1 in 20
options.rationale: Far more gave in at least once.

options.label: About 1 in 4
options.rationale: Too low: most gave in at least once.

questions.explanation: Asch found that 76 percent of participants, about three in four, conformed to the wrong answer at least once.

questions.prompt: Match each change to Asch's setup with its effect on conformity.
questions.explanation: A bigger majority raised conformity only up to a point. One ally made conformity drop sharply. A private answer lowered conformity, one reason ballots are secret.

questions.prompt: Asch's real participant never knew the others were planted. Under Level 9's research rules, what does a study like this owe participants at the end?

options.label: A bonus payment for being deceived
options.rationale: Money isn't what the rules require.

options.label: Nothing, as long as no one was physically hurt
options.rationale: Deception still has to be explained afterward.

options.label: A copy of every other participant's answers
options.rationale: The others were confederates; that isn't the requirement.

options.label: A full, honest debriefing about the deception

questions.explanation: When a study uses deception, participants get a full debriefing that honestly explains its purpose and why deception was needed.
